## Methods

Patients were eligible for inclusion in the study if they were infants younger than 6 months of age who had received a diagnosis of infantile-onset Pompe’s disease and had presented with cardiomegaly, hypotonia, and biallelic pathogenic variants in GAA. Patients with a modified Ross classification of class IV were excluded; classes range from I to IV, with higher classes indicating heart failure of greater severity.^{10} Additional inclusion and exclusion criteria are provided in the Methods section in the Supplementary Appendix. The cross-reactive immunologic material (CRIM) status of enrolled patients was predicted on the basis of genotype. Among patients with infantile-onset Pompe’s disease, CRIM status serves as an important prognostic factor; negative CRIM status is associated with worse outcomes.^{11-15}

In accordance with the experimental plan, the first patient’s case served as the sentinel case. The first patient received a single injection of GC301 and underwent a safety assessment for a minimum of 4 weeks. Additional patients could be enrolled and treated with GC301 only if the first patient did not meet the criterion for study discontinuation, which was the occurrence of a grade 3 or higher drug-related adverse event within 4 weeks after the GC301 injection. GC301 was administered at a dose of 1.2×10^{14} vector genomes per kilogram of body weight in an intravenous infusion over a period of 55 to 77 minutes. Prophylactic prednisolone was also administered.

The primary objective of the study was to assess the safety of GC301, and the secondary objective was to evaluate efficacy. Safety outcomes included adverse events and laboratory values. Psychomotor outcomes included the Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination (HINE) score (scores range from 0 to 78, with higher scores indicating better neurologic performance)^{16} and motor milestones reached on the basis of World Health Organization criteria.^{17} Cardiac outcomes included echocardiographic findings. GAA enzyme activity was measured in dried blood spots; vector genome viremia was measured in whole blood. ## Results

### Patient and Disease Characteristics

Four patients with infantile-onset Pompe’s disease were enrolled in the study (Table 1). Patient 1 received GC301 on September 6, 2022, and the other three patients were enrolled between October 9, 2022, and March 30, 2023. Three patients (Patients 2, 3, and 4) were predicted to be positive for CRIM on the basis of genotype; the prediction of CRIM status was uncertain for Patient 1 (Table S1). At the time of enrollment, each patient had received enzyme-replacement therapy with one to five infusions of rhGAA. No patients had received immune-tolerance induction therapy before enzyme-replacement therapy.

Recently, Genecradle Therapeutics' GC301 adeno-associated virus (AAV) injection for the treatment of late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) has successfully completed the first intravenous dosing in a gene therapy clinical study ("A Single-Arm, Multi-Center, Open-Label, Intravenous Phase I/II Clinical Study to Evaluate the Safety, Tolerability, and Efficacy of GC301 Adeno-Associated Virus Injection in Patients with Late-Onset Pompe Disease," Approval Number: CXSL2300013). This marks the first subject dosing in a registered clinical trial for AAV gene therapy for LOPD in China.

The gene therapy study for late-onset Pompe disease is being conducted at the First Medical Center of the General Hospital of the People's Liberation Army, with the principal investigator being Professor Yang Guang, the head of the pediatric department. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We developed a gene therapy, GC301, that delivers a codon-optimized gene encoding human acid α-glucosidase (GAA) and is mediated by recombinant AAV9 (rAAV9-coGAA) for the treatment of Pompe’s disease. This therapy has a composite promoter that comprises the cytomegalovirus early enhancer, the chicken β-actin promoter, and a 5′ untranslated region consisting of an inserted intron of the housekeeping gene TAF1 (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix, available with the full text of this article at NEJM.org); the promoter provides ubiquitous tissue expression. Our preclinical study,^{9} which explored dose-dependent GAA expression, biodistribution, and toxic effects in mice and nonhuman primate models after the injection of GC301, provided the rationale for the current work. Here, we report preliminary results regarding the safety and efficacy of treatment with GC301 in four infants with Pompe’s disease.

Enzyme-replacement therapy (ERT) was administered at a dose of 20 mg per kilogram of body weight. Our preliminary pilot clinical study (ChiCTR2200063229) of recombinant AAV9-GAA (GC301) in treatment-naïve infants with IOPD under one year of age showed promising safety and efficacy, enabling sustained independence from ERT and ventilation over one year. However, no research was performed on the application of systemic AAV9-mediated gene therapy in patients with IOPD older than one year who had already received extended prior ERT—a common real-world clinical scenario.

### Added value of this study

This single-arm, single-center study provides the first clinical evidence that a single intravenous infusion of GC301 is feasible, safe, and can confer therapeutic benefits in children with IOPD (median age 25.5 months) who had received prolonged prior ERT (median 19.5 months). It provides preliminary evidence suggesting that gene therapy can potentially be integrated following established ERT. Key findings include: (1) Sustained ERT- and ventilator-free survival in five of six patients for one year; (2) All documented children exhibited growth and development during the observation period; (3) Patients 1, 2, and 3 achieved key milestones such as unassisted crawling, standing, and walking during the observation period (the independent standing and walking of patient 1 occurred in the 13th month); (4) A consistent improvement in disease-specific quality of life; (5) Exploratory histopathological analyses of percutaneous quadriceps muscle biopsies suggested reductions in lysosomal glycogen accumulation, alongside apparent improvements in muscle integrity and mitochondrial activity; and (6) A manageable safety profile with no adverse events directly attributed to the gene therapy product.

### Implications of all the available evidence

Collectively, the evidence from preclinical studies, the initial trial in treatment-naïve infants, and this ERT-experienced cohort supports the potential of a single-dose, systemic AAV9-GAA gene therapy as a promising therapeutic avenue for IOPD. It suggests a move away from chronic, burdensome enzyme infusions towards a strategy that may mitigate some of the tissue biodistribution limitations inherent to ERT.
